video.title: He Watched This Channel and Made $32K in His First 2 Months

summary: Tyler describes starting a stump grinding service in Utah while keeping his full-time job, then going full-time after demand grew. He found early work by subcontracting for tree companies, then added homeowner jobs through Google Business Profile and reviews. He explains his pricing, equipment costs, outreach, operating routine, and some risks from underground utility lines. The hosts also discuss selling a stump grinding playbook, a possible mulch sideline, and other business paths.

ideas.name: Stump grinding service
ideas.one_liner: Grind tree stumps for homeowners and subcontract for tree companies and other outdoor trades.
ideas.business_model: Per-job service, with a minimum charge, per-inch pricing, and an extra charge for hauling chips.
ideas.customer: Homeowners with stumps, tree companies needing stump work subcontracted, and occasionally landscape installers, fence installers, or concrete contractors.
ideas.problem: Tree companies often dislike stump work because it requires separate equipment and does not fit their usual workflow; homeowners also need stumps removed after tree work or when buying a property with an untended yard.
ideas.offer: Travel to the site, grind stumps, push grindings into the resulting hole, and optionally haul away some wood chips. Tyler also cuts some taller stumps before grinding.

pricing.model: Per job, with a minimum charge and a per-inch rate; hauling is an upcharge.

price_points.label: Lowest rate Tyler had heard of in a higher-volume area
Rough quote, conditional on the described size

pricing.notes: Tyler measures the widest point of a stump. He adjusts for access, stump condition, and whether chip hauling is requested; no hauling price was stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Approached tree companies that rented stump grinders or already used a subcontractor, offering to save them time or do the work for less, better, or more reliably. He also received work from some landscape installers, fence installers, and concrete contractors.

quote.text: The people that rented or using another sub are like my prime customer. Cuz if you're renting, hey, I can save you money and a headache of doing it.
quote.speaker: Tyler

acquisition_channels.details: Built a list of local trade businesses and contacted them by text, email, or phone. In the UK, outbound texts to individuals and sole traders require consent; cold email may be used for limited companies, and cold calls need TPS/CTPS screening.

quote.text: I scraped a whole list of tree trimming businesses from all the surrounding areas from where we are here and then I started reaching out to them.
quote.speaker: Tyler

acquisition_channels.details: Homeowners found him through Google search and his local profile, which he said ranked highly after he accumulated reviews.

quote.text: This one came from Google. So they just found just organic top Google.
quote.speaker: Tyler

acquisition_channels.details: Used Google Guaranteed / LSA placements and paid per ad after completing the platform's verification process.

quote.text: I do Google guaranteed. Basically, Google guarantees the service of certain businesses by knowing that they're insured and they have they hit a certain level of requirement and then you pay per ad, but they put you at the top.
quote.speaker: Tyler

acquisition_channels.details: Contractors continued sending him work after the initial outreach; customer reviews and referrals helped sustain incoming jobs.
Posted visual stump grinding content on Twitter and received direct messages asking how to start; he converted repeated questions into a paid playbook.

quote.text: I was getting tons of DMs like, "How do you do this? How do you do this?" Really basic questions and I got really sick of hopping on every call.
quote.speaker: Tyler

ideas.delivery: Tyler personally answers calls, quotes jobs, schedules work, transports and operates the grinder, and handles the physical cleanup. He measures stumps with a tape measure, may cut some stumps with a chainsaw, grinds them, and usually pushes the chips into the hole. He charges extra when hauling is requested. He has subcontracted some tree work.
unit_economics_claims: Tyler said his minimum was $200 per visit and his local rate was about $7 per inch.
He described a $350 multi-stump job taking about 30 minutes in an open yard; a small stump alone could hit the $200 minimum.
He reported average revenue of about $300 per job and current monthly overhead of roughly $4,000 to $5,000.
He said the first two months produced $32,000 in revenue and about $26,000 in profit, though the profit figure is also stated as a rough range.
He estimated that one contractor sent him $25,000 of work over four or five months.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated as a total. Tyler initially rented equipment and later bought the stump grinder; a truck or access to one is needed. The hosts recommend renting a truck, trailer, and grinder to test demand.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Tyler said he tested his market on July 12 and completed his first stump job on August 3; the year for those dates was not stated in that passage.

acquisition.how: Google listings and paid local ads can bring inbound leads, but Tyler's early outreach and review requests were personal. His UK cold-text method would need consent or a different compliant channel.

onboarding.how: A customer can send a stump photo and diameter by text for a quote, but Tyler still assesses access, confirms price, and schedules the job.

delivery.how: Grinding, cutting, hauling, and site cleanup require a person and physical machinery at the property.

billing.how: No invoicing or payment system was described; the job price and any haul-away charge need to be agreed and collected by a person.

support.how: Tyler personally answers calls and addresses job issues, including utility damage.

uk_applicability.notes: The service can operate in the UK, but equipment, insurance, local seasonality, and utility-marking procedures would need to match the area. Acquisition should use compliant inbound channels or appropriate business-to-business outreach; unsolicited marketing texts to individuals and sole traders require consent.

risks: Physical work cannot be run unattended by software; equipment transport and operation remain central.
Tyler described damaging a pressurised sprinkler line and cutting a private electrical line. Public utility marking did not cover the private line, and the customer had told him about it.
The business is seasonal and weather-dependent; Tyler said winter work was possible locally when snow melted quickly.
Equipment depreciates, and pricing must account for machinery and transport costs rather than just labour time.
Tyler said early jobs came from contractors, so relying only on direct homeowner enquiries may leave gaps in the schedule.
In the UK, copying the described unsolicited text outreach to individuals or sole traders would require prior consent; cold calls need TPS/CTPS screening.

tactics.name: Piggyback on trades with an existing stump problem
steps: List tree companies in the surrounding service area, along with landscape installers, fence installers, and concrete contractors who sometimes encounter stumps.
Prioritise businesses that rent a grinder or already use a subcontractor.
Contact a small batch at a time so the full lead list is not used at once.
Ask whether they grind stumps themselves, subcontract the work, or own a machine.
Call businesses that respond and explain how the service could save them time or improve turnaround.

quote.text: The P stands for piggyback. So we want to piggyback off of existing businesses that have a pain point, which are tree companies that don't want to do stuff.
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Ask for a review after the job
steps: Introduce yourself to the homeowner as the stump grinding operator, even when a tree company brought you to the job.
After finishing, explain that you are growing your own company and ask directly for a review.
Make it easy for the customer to submit the review while you are there.
Keep a record of completed jobs and customer contact details so past customers can be asked later.

quote.text: Hey, I run a different company. I just started and I'm I'm working really hard to grow my company here in Utah County. Would you please give me a review?
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Make quoting simple with photos and measurements
steps: For a remote quote, ask the customer to text a photo and stump diameter.
Measure the widest point of each stump.
State a rough estimate and explain that the confirmed quote depends on the photo and measurements.
Offer the next available schedule once the customer accepts.

quote.text: If I can just text you real quick and you can text back a picture of the three stumps and just a diameter measurement. And if you get me that, that's all I need for a full quote.
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Price for travel, machine wear, and site conditions
steps: Set a minimum charge for a visit.
Use the widest stump diameter for per-inch pricing.
Account for access, stump condition, equipment depreciation, and any requested chip hauling.
Do not treat a short job as costless just because the grinding itself takes a few minutes.

quote.text: You got to be careful cuz you're not just including your own man hours. Like this is a very expensive machine and it depreciates.
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Test demand before committing to equipment
steps: Keep the existing job while testing the local market and doing early work around the work schedule.
Rent equipment at first instead of buying a grinder immediately.
Use early jobs to learn the service, gather reviews, and see whether contractors keep sending work.
Consider buying or financing a grinder after demand is clearer.

quote.text: You didn't buy the machine right away. You didn't hop into, you know, large expenses. You tested it on the side.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Win contractor work through responsiveness
steps: Answer inbound calls consistently.
Quote quickly, including by text when the job is straightforward.
Schedule promptly when a tree company needs a stump ground before it can collect payment.
Communicate immediately if something goes wrong and explain how it will be fixed.

quote.text: Responsiveness is a huge one. Second one is having the equipment that isn't the rental equipment once you get to that point.
quote.speaker: Tyler

tactics.name: Turn repeat questions into a reusable product
steps: Share visual work examples on social media.
Notice repeated questions from people asking how to start.
Write the answers into a playbook instead of repeating the same introductory call.
Use a community or course for buyers who want more guidance.

quote.text: I was getting tons of DMs like, "How do you do this? How do you do this?" Really basic questions and I got really sick of hopping on every call.
quote.speaker: Tyler
